prompt: What does a managed identity remove that a service principal with a secret has?
hint: Who holds the credential?

choices.text: The need for a role assignment
choices.why: An identity with no role reaches nothing; roles are still needed.

choices.text: A credential anybody has to store or renew
choices.why: Right. Azure holds it and rotates it.

choices.text: The entry in Entra ID
choices.why: A managed identity is a service principal in the directory.

choices.text: The access token
choices.why: The code still uses a token; it just never sees a credential.

prompt: The shop's pipeline runs on GitHub's machines and must deploy to Azure. Can it use a managed identity?
hint: Where does the code have to run?

choices.text: Yes, a user-assigned one, since it is a resource of its own
choices.why: Being a resource does not let it be used from outside Azure.

choices.text: Yes, once the repository is linked to the subscription
choices.why: No such link turns GitHub into an Azure resource.

choices.text: No: it is not on Azure, so lesson 7's federation is the answer
choices.why: Right. Managed identities serve code running on Azure resources.

choices.text: No: managed identities serve virtual machines only
choices.why: App Service, Functions, Container Apps and AKS use them too.

prompt: The web app `app-shop-prod` is deleted and recreated by a deployment. What happens to its system-assigned identity's roles?
hint: Whose lifetime does it follow?

choices.text: They are gone; the new identity starts with none
choices.why: Right. The deployment has to give them again.

choices.text: They move to the new web app automatically
choices.why: The new app has a new identity, a new principal.

choices.text: They stay, attached to the old identity's name
choices.why: Roles point at object ids, and the old one is deleted.

choices.text: They are restored from the subscription's backup
choices.why: No such backup of role assignments exists.

prompt: Why does the shop give its roles to `id-shop-app`, a user-assigned identity?
hint: It outlives the apps.

choices.text: Because system-assigned identities cannot hold roles
choices.why: They can; they just lose them with their resource.

choices.text: Because user-assigned identities are free and system ones are not
choices.why: Price is not the difference the lesson draws.

choices.text: Because it signs in with a certificate
choices.why: No managed identity hands anybody a certificate.

choices.text: Every new copy of the app starts with the roles
choices.why: Right. Given once, kept across rebuilds, shared by many resources.

prompt: In the compiled template, `systemPrincipalId` is a `reference(...)` expression rather than a GUID. Why?
hint: When does the GUID come into existence?

choices.text: Outputs are always expressions in ARM templates
choices.why: An output can be a plain value; this one cannot be known yet.

choices.text: Bicep hides principal ids for security
choices.why: A principal id is not secret; it does not exist yet.

choices.text: The compiler failed to find the web app
choices.why: It found it; the expression names it.

choices.text: Entra ID makes it when the identity is created
choices.why: Right. The template can only say where to read it afterwards.

prompt: Which of these are true of a user-assigned identity? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare the two columns of the table.

choices.text: It can be given roles before any resource uses it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Several resources can share it
choices.why: Right: one principal, a short role list.

choices.text: It is deleted with the first resource that used it
choices.why: That is the system-assigned kind.

choices.text: It is a resource of type `userAssignedIdentities`
choices.why: Right, as in `app.bicep`.

choices.text: It works for code outside Azure
choices.why: No managed identity does; that is federation.

prompt: Where does code on an Azure virtual machine ask for its managed identity's token?
hint: A link-local address.

choices.text: At the metadata service, `169.254.169.254`
choices.why: Right. Only that machine can reach it.

choices.text: At `login.microsoftonline.com`, with the machine's secret
choices.why: The machine holds no secret; the platform signs in for it.

choices.text: At `management.azure.com`
choices.why: That is where the token is used, not where it is obtained.

choices.text: In a file the platform writes to the disk
choices.why: That is workload identity in Kubernetes, not a VM.

prompt: Why does the metadata service refuse a request without the header `Metadata: true`?
hint: Think of a server tricked into fetching a URL.

choices.text: To tell version 2018 requests from older ones
choices.why: That is `api-version`'s job.

choices.text: A fetch forced through a crafted URL cannot add it
choices.why: Right. It keeps a request a page tricks the server into making from reaching the token.

choices.text: Because plain HTTP needs a header to be secure
choices.why: The request never leaves the host; HTTP is enough.

choices.text: To choose which managed identity answers
choices.why: That is the `client_id` parameter.

prompt: The web app has both identities. `id-shop-app` holds Storage Blob Data Reader on the account, but reads are refused. `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` was left out of the app's settings. What is happening?
hint: Which identity answers a request that names none?

choices.text: The role takes a day to apply
choices.why: That is not the explanation the evidence points to.

choices.text: User-assigned identities cannot read storage
choices.why: They can, given the role, as `app.bicep` does.

choices.text: The code signs in as the system-assigned identity, which has no role
choices.why: Right. Check the token's `oid` before blaming the role.

choices.text: The storage account refuses tokens from App Service
choices.why: It accepts any token with the right role.

prompt: Why is a managed identity "exactly as safe as the machine it is attached to"?
hint: The credential cannot leak. What can?

choices.text: Any code running there can ask for a token
choices.why: Right. Hence the narrowest roles on the narrowest scope.

choices.text: Because the machine can change the identity's roles
choices.why: Roles are changed in Azure, not from the machine.

choices.text: Because Entra ID trusts the machine's IP address
choices.why: Nothing in the flow trusts an address.

choices.text: Because its credential is stored on the machine's disk
choices.why: No credential is on the machine at all.

prompt: Match each part of the metadata request to what it does.
hint: Five parts in the table, four here.

pairs.right: which API the token is for
which identity, when there are several
proof the request was made on purpose

prompt: App Service gives the address of its identity service in the environment variable `IDENTITY____`.
hint: Its partner is `IDENTITY_HEADER`.

prompt: What does `DefaultAzureCredential` do?
hint: A list.

choices.text: Signs in as the subscription's owner by default
choices.why: It signs in as whatever credential it finds first.

choices.text: Asks the user to choose a credential
choices.why: It chooses by its fixed order, unattended.

choices.text: Creates a managed identity when none exists
choices.why: It creates nothing; it only looks.

choices.text: Tries a fixed list of credentials in order
choices.why: Right. The first that produces a token wins.

prompt: Put these credentials in the order `DefaultAzureCredential` tries them.
hint: The lab printed the list.
trap: The CLI comes after the managed identity: on Azure the platform answers before a developer's sign-in could.

prompt: With the three `AZURE_*` variables set, why was only `EnvironmentCredential` tried?
hint: Unavailable and failed are different outcomes.

choices.text: Because the others need a network the lab lacks
choices.why: The first run tried all of them on the same network.

choices.text: A credential that is configured and fails stops the chain
choices.why: Right. Carrying on would hide the mistake behind another identity.

choices.text: Because the variables switched the others off
choices.why: Nothing switched them off; the chain stopped.

choices.text: Because the secret was accepted and the tenant refused
choices.why: The secret was never sent; discovery failed first.

prompt: A container image built by a developer carries an old `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET` and its two partners. In production, on a resource with a managed identity, what does `DefaultAzureCredential` do?
hint: Which credential comes first?

choices.text: Uses the managed identity, which always wins on Azure
choices.why: It is third in the list; the environment comes first.

choices.text: Refuses to start until the variables are removed
choices.why: Nothing checks for that; it simply uses them.

choices.text: Signs in as the old service principal, with its roles
choices.why: Right, if the secret still works. Name the credential you mean in production.

choices.text: Tries both and keeps the one with more roles
choices.why: It stops at the first that answers.

prompt: What does the lesson recommend for code that runs only in production, on a resource with a user-assigned identity?
hint: One line in place of the default list.

choices.text: `DefaultAzureCredential`, since it adapts to anything
choices.why: Adapting is the danger when a stray credential is present.

choices.text: `AzureCliCredential`, with `az login` run at start-up
choices.why: That would need a stored credential to sign in with.

choices.text: `ManagedIdentityCredential(client_id=...)`
choices.why: Right. It cannot fall through to anything else.

choices.text: `EnvironmentCredential`, with the client id in a variable
choices.why: That one needs a secret or certificate, which is what is avoided.

prompt: How many credentials did `DefaultAzureCredential` list as attempted in the lab's first run?
hint: Count the lines under *Attempted credentials*.

prompt: Put the steps of the shop's web app reading an image with `id-shop-app` in order.
hint: The role is given before anything asks for a token.
items: give it Storage Blob Data Reader on the storage account
attach it to the web app and set `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`
the code asks the platform for a token naming that client id
the code reads the blob with the token
trap: A user-assigned identity can take its role before it is attached, which is one of its advantages.

prompt: A team moves an application from a virtual machine to their laptops for debugging, with the same code using `DefaultAzureCredential`. What identity does it use there, and why is that fine?
hint: Which credential answers on a laptop?

choices.text: The developer's own `az login`, with her own roles
choices.why: Right. The same code signs in as whoever runs it, which is the point of the class.

choices.text: The VM's managed identity, reached over the internet
choices.why: The metadata service is link-local; a laptop cannot reach it.

choices.text: None: the code must be changed for laptops
choices.why: Not changing the code is what the class is for.

choices.text: A copy of the managed identity's secret
choices.why: There is no such secret to copy.

prompt: A token's ___ claim holds the object id of the principal that signed in.
hint: Three letters.
